lessons.title: Text, numbers and small checks
lessons.subtitle: Choose the right representation before calculating or matching.
rules: `int` and `long` are whole numbers; `double` uses binary floating point; `decimal` suits decimal arithmetic.
Integer division drops the fraction. Convert before dividing; combine totals before calculating a combined ratio.
`$"Hi {name}"` interpolates; `@"a\b"` keeps backslashes; raw strings use three or more quotation marks.
`is` and `switch` patterns inspect values or shapes. Regular expressions inspect patterns inside text.
`values[^1]` means last. An array range copies elements; slicing a `Span<T>` creates a view.
lessons.python:
done_a, total_a = 1, 2
done_b, total_b = 9, 10
combined = (done_a + done_b) / (total_a + total_b)
print(combined > 0.8)
# Python / keeps a fraction; use Decimal for decimal arithmetic.

reference.meaning: `int`: 32-bit signed; `long`: 64-bit signed, e.g. `9L`. `0.5` is double; `0.5m` is decimal. Neither makes every fraction exact.
`new DateOnly(2026, 9, 8)` is a calendar date, with no time or timezone. Comparable to Python datetime.date.
`new StringBuilder().Append("a").Append("b").ToString()` builds text through a mutable buffer; useful for repeated additions.
`"""{"name":"Ava"}"""` holds JSON text without escaping its internal quotes. Multiline raw strings use delimiter placement and indentation rules.
`name is { Length: > 0 }` checks a non-null value and its property. `items is [1, ..]` checks a list starting with 1.
`count switch { 0 => "none", 1 => "one", _ => "many" }` selects a result; `_` is the fallback.
`Regex.IsMatch(text, @"\A\d+\z")` checks that the entire text contains one or more digits. The regex library interprets this string.
`values[1..3]` includes indexes 1 and 2; the end is excluded. A mutable span view shares the original array storage.
Averaging 1/2 and 9/10 gives 0.7. Combined progress is 10/12, about 0.8333. Check for a zero denominator.
`enum Size { Small, Large }` defines named constants in a distinct value type. Use `Size.Small`; an enum is not a string or a class instance.

lessons.trap: Python integer / produces a fraction; C# int / int produces an integer. Casting the already-truncated answer is too late.
lessons.agentConnection: The generated applications format text, match input shapes, parse dates and calculate evidence from totals using these ordinary operations.

questions.prompt: What is printed?

options.why: Correct: both operands are int, so division truncates the fraction.
That needs a decimal or floating-point operand, such as 5m / 2.
Integer division is legal; it just has different semantics from Python /.

questions.hint: Look at the operand types, not the variable name.
questions.explanation: C# calculates 5 / 2 using integer division. Use 5m / 2 or (decimal)5 / 2 for a decimal fraction.

verification.program:
using System;
Console.WriteLine(5 / 2);

questions.prompt: Which one-character prefix inserts the value of name into this string?
questions.hint: This is the C# counterpart of the prefix on a Python f-string.
questions.explanation: The $ prefix enables interpolation. Without it, braces are literal text. @ controls backslash handling instead.

questions.prompt: Which value is printed after changing a copy and a view?

options.why: The original second item starts as 4, but the span assignment changes it.
8 was assigned to the separate array copy.
Correct: the span shares storage with values, so view[0] changes values[1].

questions.hint: The copy owns a new array; the span refers to the old array.
questions.explanation: An array range creates a shallow element copy. AsSpan creates a view. For int elements, editing the copy cannot change the original.

questions.prompt: What do these two C# patterns print?

options.why: Correct: the list has two matching elements and the string has Length 4.
The > 3 relational pattern matches 4, so the list test succeeds too.
These are C# list/property patterns, not regex strings.

questions.hint: Square brackets here describe list shape; braces describe properties.
questions.explanation: [2, > 3] matches exactly two elements: 2 followed by a number greater than 3. { Length: 4 } checks a non-null object with that property value.

lessons.title: A task is a promise of completion
lessons.subtitle: Read asynchronous code without imagining a new thread for every call.
rules: `Task` tracks completion, failure or cancellation. `Task<T>` also supplies a successful result of type T.
`async` enables `await`. Await obtains the result or propagates an exception; an incomplete await can suspend the method.
Calling a normal C# async method starts it immediately, until an incomplete await. A Python coroutine call behaves differently.
`Task.WhenAll` represents completion of every supplied task. It does not promise separate threads.
An already-completed task needs no suspension. Prefer await over blocking `.Result` or `.Wait()`.
lessons.python:
import asyncio

async def double(number):
    return number * 2

# Inside async Python code:
pending = double(3)  # a coroutine; body has not started
result = await pending
# asyncio.create_task(double(3)) schedules it to run.

reference.meaning: The example prints entered, called, 6. The call executes the method body; awaiting CompletedTask does not pause it.
Start independent operations, then await Task.WhenAll(a, b). Their waits may overlap. CPU parallelism requires separate consideration.
For Task<T> inputs, the resulting array follows input task order, even if operations finish in another order.
asyncio.gather waits for multiple awaitables. Python create_task schedules a coroutine; it does not synchronously run its body by default.
Normal async APIs return already-started operations. An explicitly constructed new Task(...) can be unstarted; that is not the pattern taught here.

A value-type awaitable used by some library APIs: `int n = await ReadAsync();`. Consume each returned ValueTask once; it may avoid a Task allocation for synchronous completion, but is not a universal optimization.

lessons.trap: A task is neither its eventual value nor a dedicated thread. Await can resume immediately when the task is complete.
lessons.agentConnection: Agent request methods await model calls and tool work; they can suspend while waiting without creating one thread per request.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes Task<int>?

options.text: It is always an int available immediately
options.why: The result may not be available yet; the task also tracks failure or cancellation.

options.text: It represents completion and can produce an int
options.why: Correct: await obtains the int when the task completes successfully.

options.text: It guarantees a separate worker thread
options.why: A Task describes an operation, not a guaranteed thread.

questions.hint: Separate the container for completion from the successful value.
questions.explanation: Task<int> describes an asynchronous operation with an int result. The task can also complete unsuccessfully.

questions.prompt: Fill the keyword that obtains the int asynchronously.
questions.hint: The successful value is inside Task<int>.
questions.explanation: Await unwraps the successful result. If the task fails, await propagates its exception instead.

questions.prompt: What is printed, and what does WhenAll guarantee?

options.why: Correct: the values follow the order supplied to WhenAll.
WhenAll returns results in input order, not reverse order.

options.text: 2,5; each operation has its own thread
options.why: The output is right, but Task.WhenAll provides no thread-per-task guarantee.

questions.hint: The returned array follows input order.
questions.explanation: WhenAll waits for all supplied tasks. These example tasks are already completed; no background worker is needed.

questions.prompt: Order these statements so each value exists before it is used.
questions.hint: First create the task, then obtain its result, then use the result.
questions.explanation: The await depends on pending, and the output depends on number. This order prints 8.

lessons.title: Stop requests and clean up
lessons.subtitle: Cancellation is cooperative; cleanup belongs to a clear scope.
rules: `CancellationTokenSource` requests cancellation; its token lets work observe that request.
`CancelAfter` requests cancellation after a deadline. Linked sources combine multiple cancellation requests.
Pass the token into cancellable operations or call `ThrowIfCancellationRequested`; cancellation does not forcibly kill work.
`using var` disposes at scope exit. `await using` awaits asynchronous disposal. Garbage collection serves a different purpose.
`catch` handles exceptions; `when` filters a catch. `finally` runs when leaving the try/catch construct, after any matching catch.
lessons.python:
try:
    raise ValueError("stop this example")
except ValueError:
    print("caught")
finally:
    print("cleanup")
# Python with / async with resemble scoped cleanup.
# C# CancellationToken is not Python task.cancel().

reference.meaning: `using var linked = CancellationTokenSource.CreateLinkedTokenSource(callerToken, deadlineToken);` creates a source cancelled when either input cancels.
`stop.CancelAfter(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5))` schedules a request. Work that ignores its token can continue beyond that time.
Dispose releases resources or completes a scope promptly. The garbage collector later reclaims managed memory; using does not force collection.
`await using var resource = ...;` awaits DisposeAsync at scope exit; the resource must support asynchronous disposal.
A failing async method normally faults its task. Await rethrows the failure at the await expression; surrounding catch can handle it.
`catch (OperationCanceledException) when (token.IsCancellationRequested)` handles that type only if the condition is true. Otherwise the search continues.
Inside catch, `throw;` rethrows while preserving the original exception stack. Do not catch errors merely to hide them.

lessons.trap: Calling Cancel requests a stop; disposing a CancellationTokenSource cleans it up but does not itself request cancellation.
lessons.agentConnection: Requests use deadlines and browser-disconnect tokens, while using/finally scopes close resources and tracing spans on success or failure.

questions.prompt: You call stop.Cancel(), but a long loop never checks the token. What is guaranteed?

options.why: CancellationTokenSource does not forcibly interrupt arbitrary code.
Correct: the loop must cooperate by observing the token or using a cancellable API.
A cancellation request is not a process-termination command.

questions.hint: A token is a signal, not a kill switch.
questions.explanation: Cooperative work checks the token or passes it to operations that do. Without cooperation, the loop can continue.

questions.prompt: What is the order of the three output lines?

options.why: Correct: using disposes Marker when control leaves its enclosing block.
The resource is disposed after its use, not when created.
The inner block ends before after is printed, so disposal happens first.

questions.hint: Find the closing brace of the scope containing using var.
questions.explanation: The compiler arranges disposal at scope exit, including normal exception unwinding. This does not depend on garbage collection.

questions.prompt: Fill the method name that schedules a cancellation request after five seconds.
questions.hint: This sets a deadline on the source; it does not sleep here.
questions.explanation: CancelAfter schedules cancellation. Passing stop.Token into work is still necessary for that work to observe it.
questions.code:
using var stop = new CancellationTokenSource();
stop.__(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5));

questions.prompt: What is printed when this task fails?

options.why: Await propagates the failure, so execution skips the success line.
Correct: await throws the task failure into catch, then finally runs.

options.text: Nothing; Task failures cannot be caught
options.why: Await makes failures observable through ordinary try/catch.

questions.hint: Follow the exception at the await expression.
questions.explanation: The faulted task throws InvalidOperationException when awaited. The matching catch handles it; finally runs afterward.

lessons.title: One value at a time
lessons.subtitle: A sequence can do work when you ask for the next value.
rules: An `IEnumerable<T>` iterator uses `yield return`; its body runs during enumeration, not when the iterator is obtained.
`IAsyncEnumerable<T>` allows waiting between elements. Consume it with `await foreach`.
`WithCancellation(token)` supplies an enumeration token; `[EnumeratorCancellation]` connects it to an async iterator parameter.
`ConfigureAwait(false)` avoids requesting the captured context. It does not choose or create a background thread.
`foreach` and `await foreach` dispose supported enumerators when their loops exit, including early break.
lessons.python:
import asyncio

async def count():
    yield 1
    await asyncio.sleep(0)
    yield 2

# Inside async Python code:
# async for number in count():
#     print(number)

reference.meaning: Calling an async iterator obtains a sequence without executing its body. Enumeration drives that body, unlike a normal async Task method.
An iterator may rerun its body on each enumeration. Storing IEnumerable<T> does not materialize its results.
A stream can deliver values as they become available. A Task<List<T>> produces a complete list before the caller receives its result.
Use `async IAsyncEnumerable<int> Read([EnumeratorCancellation] CancellationToken token = default)`. Check token or pass it to awaited work.
`await foreach (var x in Read().WithCancellation(token))` passes the token to enumeration. The producer must consume it.
`await operation.ConfigureAwait(false)` controls continuation-context capture for that await. ASP.NET Core normally has no custom synchronization context.
The loop awaits asynchronous enumerator disposal. A producer finally block can run then. This does not finish producing remaining values.

lessons.trap: An async iterator does not make the HTTP response streaming by itself. The server and browser must also exchange and consume chunks.
lessons.agentConnection: Model updates and browser NDJSON can be consumed incrementally; other routes collect the stream before returning one complete response.

questions.prompt: Which line appears first?

options.why: Calling an iterator creates the enumerable; it does not run its iterator body yet.
Correct: enumeration begins only at foreach.
The body prints started before yielding its first value.

questions.hint: Find the first statement that asks the sequence for an element.
questions.explanation: The full output is made query, started, 1. IEnumerable describes a sequence; enumeration performs the work.

questions.prompt: Which keyword completes a loop over an IAsyncEnumerable<int>?
questions.hint: The next value may require an asynchronous wait.
questions.explanation: await foreach can await each move to the next value and asynchronously dispose the enumerator when the loop exits.

questions.prompt: What is printed when the consumer breaks after one value?

options.why: break stops consumption; the producer does not continue to yield 2.
The async iterator is disposed, so its finally block also runs.
Correct: early exit disposes the enumerator and executes its cleanup.

questions.hint: A loop still performs enumerator cleanup when break exits it.
questions.explanation: The consumer sees 1, then breaks. await foreach disposes the async iterator, which executes finally without yielding 2.

questions.prompt: What does ConfigureAwait(false) mean?

options.text: Always resume on a new background thread
options.why: It does not promise any specific thread or create one.

options.text: Do not request resumption on the captured context
options.why: Correct: it controls context capture, not the existence of a background worker.
Cancellation and exceptions still propagate through await.

questions.hint: It configures the await continuation, not the operation result.
questions.explanation: ConfigureAwait(false) avoids requesting the captured context. If the awaitable is already complete, execution may simply continue synchronously.

lessons.title: Project files, paths and settings
lessons.subtitle: Distinguish compilation, runtime files, and values chosen at startup.
rules: Namespaces group type names. `using System.Text;` imports names for lookup; it does not create objects or dispose resources.
`Path.Combine` joins path parts. `AppContext.BaseDirectory` locates the application base, which can differ from the working directory.
The `.csproj` declares target framework, packages and copied content. NuGet supplies packages; using directives do not install them.
`IConfiguration` reads settings through providers. For the same key, the provider added later takes precedence.
Inspect the actual provider order. Keep credentials separate from ordinary settings, committed sample files and printed output.

reference.meaning: The SDK includes compiler and build tools. `dotnet build` compiles the project; `dotnet run` builds as needed and starts it.
.NET runs compiled C# code. ASP.NET Core adds web hosting, HTTP routes and middleware; they are framework capabilities.
A `.csproj` PackageReference names a NuGet dependency and version. Restore resolves it; a namespace import only shortens source names.
Inside ItemGroup, `<None Update="Data/*.json" CopyToOutputDirectory="PreserveNewest" />` copies matching existing project items into build output.
Use CopyToPublishDirectory when content must be included in published output. Verify deployed paths; build output and publishing are different stages.
`Path.Combine(AppContext.BaseDirectory, "Data", "colors.json")` locates deployed content without assuming the shell started in the project folder.
Providers may read JSON, environment variables, command-line arguments or other sources. Framework defaults and explicit Add... calls determine order.
`namespace Learning;` assigns type names to a namespace. Folder names are a convention and do not automatically define namespaces.
The example uses Microsoft.Extensions.Configuration from the ASP.NET Core shared framework; it reads only in-memory dictionaries.

lessons.trap: Changing your current working directory can break relative file paths. Merely putting a data file beside source does not guarantee deployment.
lessons.agentConnection: Generated apps copy their local data into output, resolve it at startup and load model/observability configuration through explicit provider calls.

questions.prompt: Why does this configuration return green for Color?

options.why: The example has no environment provider, and precedence is determined by actual provider order.

options.text: The later provider supplies the same key
options.why: Correct: the green provider was added after the blue provider.
Configuration compares keys, not alphabetic order of values.

questions.hint: Read the order of AddInMemoryCollection calls.
questions.explanation: Later-added providers override earlier values for the same key. There is no universal rule that a particular source always wins.

questions.prompt: Fill the property for a path relative to the application base, independent of the shell working directory.
questions.hint: This is a property of AppContext.
questions.explanation: AppContext.BaseDirectory identifies the application base. Path.Combine joins it with portable path segments; the file still must be deployed.

questions.prompt: What does using System.Text; do?

options.why: Package references and restore handle dependencies, not using directives.

options.text: Imports a namespace for shorter type names
options.why: Correct: you can write StringBuilder instead of System.Text.StringBuilder.

options.text: Disposes all strings at scope exit
options.why: That confuses a namespace using directive with a using resource declaration.

questions.hint: Compare using System.Text; with using var resource = ...;.
questions.explanation: The same keyword has distinct roles. A using directive controls name lookup; a using declaration schedules resource disposal.

questions.prompt: Order the minimum workflow for building and running a C# project from source.
lines: Declare project target and dependencies in the .csproj.
Restore dependencies and compile the source with dotnet build.
Execute the compiled application with the .NET runtime.
questions.hint: The build needs project information; execution needs compiled output.
questions.explanation: dotnet build normally includes restore. dotnet run can perform the build stage for you, then launch the result; these are still different stages.

lessons.title: Objects cross the JSON boundary
lessons.subtitle: A typed shape helps you read data; validation decides whether to accept it.
rules: `Serialize` turns an object into JSON text; `Deserialize<T>` attempts to build a T from JSON.
A DTO is a data-transfer shape, often a record. It is not automatically a complete validation policy.
Nullable annotations guide compiler analysis. Runtime input still needs explicit checks and appropriate serializer options.
Attributes attach metadata. Reflection lets code inspect types, methods and metadata; libraries decide how to use it.
JSON source generation creates serializer support during compilation. `partial` lets generated and handwritten declarations form one type.
lessons.python:
import json

person = json.loads('{"Name":"Mira","Age":7}')
if not person.get("Name") or person["Age"] < 0:
    raise ValueError("Invalid person")
print(person["Name"])
# Python returns a dictionary here, not a typed C# record.

reference.meaning: `JsonSerializer.Serialize(new Person("Mira", 7))` creates JSON text. Property naming and enum handling depend on configured options.
System.Text.Json can opt into limited RespectNullableAnnotations checks. That still does not validate every missing value or business rule.
`[Description("Counts beads")]` describes a method. It cannot execute the method, validate its arguments or expose it as a tool by itself.
`typeof(Counter).GetMethods()` inspects method metadata at runtime. A library may use it to build tool descriptions or invoke registered methods.
`[JsonSerializable(typeof(Person))] partial class PeopleJson : JsonSerializerContext { }` requests generated JSON metadata/support.
Pass `PeopleJson.Default.Person` to the appropriate JsonSerializer overload. Declaring a context alone does not redirect every serializer call.
The C# compiler can generate serializer source. A packaging script can copy skill files. These are separate operations with different owners.

lessons.trap: A property declared string can still receive invalid external data. Types, serializer settings and application validation each do different jobs.
lessons.agentConnection: Browser DTOs and model tool arguments cross JSON boundaries; attributes describe tools and generated serializer contexts support selected data types.

questions.prompt: A method has [Description("Adds two numbers")]. What does the attribute do by itself?

options.why: Correct: another piece of code must inspect or use that metadata.
Tool exposure requires explicit framework or application registration.
DescriptionAttribute is descriptive, not an argument-validation rule.

questions.hint: An attribute is information attached to a declaration.
questions.explanation: Libraries can read Description metadata when constructing tool definitions. The C# attribute alone neither runs the method nor validates its input.

questions.prompt: What is printed when the JSON value itself is null?

options.why: Correct: deserializing JSON null into this reference type produces a null reference.
A DTO declaration does not force the JSON value to contain an object.
No Person object with a name is created from JSON null.

questions.hint: The input is the JSON null value, not an empty object.
questions.explanation: Deserialize<Person> can return null. Checking the result remains necessary before accessing members.

questions.prompt: Order this safe input path before using a value supplied from outside.
lines: Parse JSON into the expected DTO shape.
Validate presence, allowed values and domain constraints.
Use the validated data in the operation.
questions.hint: Parsing tells you the shape; validation determines acceptance.
questions.explanation: A successfully parsed object can still have invalid contents. Validation belongs before the operation that relies on those contents.

questions.prompt: Which modifier allows a generator to contribute the rest of this context type?
questions.hint: The declaration is one part of the final type.
questions.explanation: partial declarations combine at compilation. The JSON generator supplies additional implementation for the same type; this is not file-copy packaging.

lessons.title: The browser talks HTTP
lessons.subtitle: Separate browser JavaScript, server C#, and the format on the wire.
rules: ASP.NET Core maps HTTP routes to handlers. Binding turns request values into handler arguments.
Validate input before acting. `Results.Ok` creates a 200 response; `Results.BadRequest` creates a 400 response.
Middleware surrounds request handling and can continue to the next step or return a response early.
Browser JavaScript uses fetch to send HTTP requests. The browser does not directly call an ordinary C# method.
A process can serve many requests. Session state spans requests only when the application deliberately stores and identifies it.
lessons.python:
# Analogy inside a Python web framework:
# @app.get("/square/{value}")
# def square(value: int):
#     ...validate value...
#     return {"answer": value * value}
# Routing and HTTP responses come from the framework,
# not Python or C# syntax alone.

reference.meaning: A route placeholder can bind an int; a POST body can bind a DTO; registered services can be injected as parameters.
In /square/{value:int}, the int route constraint helps choose a matching route. It does not enforce the allowed 0–100 range.
Returning Results.Ok(new { answer = 9 }) lets the framework execute an HTTP result and serialize its body. A return value is not automatically a network write at that exact line.
`app.Use(async (context, next) => { /* before */ await next(context); /* after */ });` illustrates code around the next request stage.
`const response = await fetch(url); const data = await response.json();` waits for the response body and parses one JSON document. Check response.ok explicitly.
Newline-delimited JSON sends one JSON value per line. Browser code must buffer chunks until complete lines arrive; chunk boundaries need not match lines.
Server-sent events have their own text framing, such as data: lines and blank-line separators. A provider SSE stream and a browser NDJSON stream are separate protocols.
Startup-created objects may live for the process. Local handler variables live for that request. Conversation/session data needs an explicit storage policy.
This ASP.NET Core excerpt only registers a handler. A complete web app calls app.Run() to listen; the learning game starts no server.

lessons.trap: Streaming inside the server does not guarantee streaming to the browser. The HTTP route and JavaScript consumer decide that boundary.
lessons.agentConnection: The agent UIs use fetch; server endpoints validate DTOs, execute request-specific work and return JSON or explicitly framed incremental results.

questions.prompt: Which response should this handler return for /square/-2?

options.why: The request matches the int route, but the explicit range validation rejects -2.
Correct: the handler returns Results.BadRequest for negative values.

options.text: A C# compiler error in the browser
options.why: C# runs on the server; the browser sends an HTTP request.

questions.hint: A value can be a valid int but still outside your permitted range.
questions.explanation: Binding and validation are different. The route supplies -2 as an int; the handler checks its range and creates a 400 result.

questions.prompt: An NDJSON response arrives in chunks that split a JSON line in half. What should the browser do?

options.text: Parse every network chunk as a complete JSON object
options.why: Chunks can cut through a JSON token or contain several complete lines.

options.text: Buffer partial text until it has a complete line, then parse that line
options.why: Correct: NDJSON framing depends on complete lines, not network chunk boundaries.

options.text: Run the C# JSON serializer in the browser automatically
options.why: Ordinary browser JavaScript does not automatically execute server C# serializers.

questions.hint: Transport chunks and logical records are different boundaries.
questions.explanation: The consumer retains incomplete text between reads and parses complete NDJSON lines. Provider-side SSE requires its own framing parser.

questions.prompt: Order the normal single-JSON browser request path.
lines: Browser JavaScript sends an HTTP request with fetch.
Server binds and validates the request, then performs the handler work.
Server returns an HTTP response containing JSON.
Browser parses the response and updates the page.
questions.hint: Separate the two programs and the messages between them.
questions.explanation: The browser and server communicate across HTTP. Updating the browser page is JavaScript work after the response arrives.

questions.prompt: A local list is created inside each route-handler call. Will it automatically remember the previous request?

options.text: Yes; every variable in a web app is a session variable
options.why: A local variable is not automatically shared across handler calls.

options.text: No; persistent state requires deliberate storage and lifetime
options.why: Correct: new handler calls create their own locals unless code explicitly shares state.

options.text: Yes; async makes all variables global
options.why: async changes how a method waits, not the scope of its variables.

questions.hint: Think about calling an ordinary function twice.
questions.explanation: Process, request and session lifetimes are distinct. State must be placed and keyed intentionally if it should survive across requests.

lessons.title: Small functions, clear dependencies
lessons.subtitle: Keep calculation understandable; put external systems around it.
rules: A model tool is an ordinary function exposed through library registration and metadata. Tool execution is application code.
Passing a dependency into a constructor or method is dependency injection; a container can automate constructing and supplying it.
Container lifetimes choose reuse: singleton per container, scoped per scope, transient per resolution.
`ActivitySource.StartActivity` may return null. Use scoped disposal and record useful metadata without secrets or sensitive content.
Offline tests prove local behavior with controlled dependencies. Live smokes check real integration; neither proves every possible outcome.
lessons.python:
def describe(count):
    return f"{count()} beads"

print(describe(lambda: 3))
# Python can inject a function directly.
# C# also supports delegates; ICounter demonstrates
# an explicit contract with a replaceable object.

reference.meaning: `static int Add(int a, int b) => a + b;` is ordinary calculation. A tool wrapper adds a callable schema, arguments and dispatch around it.
The real agents depend on a chat-client interface. ICounter is a tiny stand-in for the same principle: supply an implementation of a contract.
`new Greeter(counter)` is manual injection. Registering ICounter and resolving Greeter lets a DI container supply that constructor argument.
One instance is reused per container. In a web app it can be used by simultaneous requests; the lifetime does not make mutable code thread-safe.
Scoped means one instance per explicit scope, commonly one HTTP request. Transient means a fresh instance each time the container resolves it.
`using var activity = source.StartActivity("count"); activity?.SetTag("item.count", 3);` marks a bounded operation when tracing is enabled.
Counts, durations and status can explain work without logging raw prompts, private text or credentials. A created Activity does not prove remote export.
The example supplies FixedCounter. An offline test can assert Describe returns 3 beads without calling a service; a live service check is separate.
`lock (gate) { count++; }` protects a critical section from other threads using the same gate. Keep it short; C# forbids await inside lock.
`Interlocked.Increment(ref count)` makes that single increment atomic. Ordinary count++ is not atomic; an atomic increment does not protect a larger sequence of operations.

lessons.trap: An interface or model-tool attribute does not add intelligence or reliability by itself. The implementation, validation and tests still determine behavior.
lessons.agentConnection: The generated agents combine deterministic tools with replaceable clients and metadata tracing. Their offline tests and live model checks cover different boundaries.

questions.prompt: What turns an ordinary Add method into a callable model tool?

options.text: Naming the method with the word Tool
options.why: Names alone cannot expose methods to an external model.

options.text: Registering a wrapper/schema and dispatching model arguments to it
options.why: Correct: framework/application code connects the model call to the ordinary method.

options.text: The C# compiler automatically calls every public method
options.why: Public access does not automatically register or invoke methods.

questions.hint: The model needs a description and the application needs a dispatch path.
questions.explanation: The deterministic function still runs as C#. Library registration supplies a tool definition and invocation plumbing; C# has no magic model-tool keyword.

questions.prompt: Which DI lifetime normally provides one service instance per HTTP request scope?

options.why: A singleton is reused across scopes in that container, potentially across many requests.
Correct: ASP.NET Core normally creates a DI scope for each HTTP request.
Transient creates a new instance per resolution, including multiple resolutions within one request.

questions.hint: The request is a common example of a scope.
questions.explanation: Scoped services are reused within their scope. Singleton and transient represent different reuse policies, not different inheritance rules.

questions.prompt: A local test supplies a fake counter that always returns 3, and the assertion passes. What does that establish?

options.text: The tested code behaves correctly with that controlled dependency
options.why: Correct: the fake makes the dependency predictable for this local assertion.
